doc.title: James Moody interviewed by Monk Rowe, San Diego, California, February 13, 1998

title: Joining Dizzy Gillespie's band in 1946
summary: He recalls the band personnel and that he did not realize what he was part of.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Playing with and understanding Thelonious Monk

blocks.x: But you see what I’m saying though? And like if a kid sees something, and you show it to him, and he can do it slowly, and — oh, I see that. It’s simple. They call it the light bulb going on. And I always say this, like I’ve been kind of fortunate, because if I explain something to you this way and you don’t get it, I can explain it four, five, six different other ways, like I think I can, because I’ve been pretty fortunate I’ve been able to do that. Because I hate for someone to come to me for someone, and I’m trying to show them, and they don’t get anything out of it. But, like you said about the bebop thing, people said well how did you feel playing bebop when you joined Dizzy’s band? When I joined Dizzy’s band in ‘46 it was I think, Monk was the piano player, Thelonious Monk, and Kenny Clarke was the drummer, Ray Brown bass, Milton Jackson vibraharp and Mr. Howard Johnson, lead alto, and Sol was the baritone player and then later Cecil Payne came in. Ernie Henry and then later John Brown, Dave Burns, Miles was in the band, Fats Navarro. I mean but I was young. I didn’t — hey man, I was there — I thought I was going to sneeze, I think I will, hold it one moment — all this is cool, no it goes along with it.
That’s right. This is live. © Fillius Jazz Archive -10-

[Sneezes] Thank you, honey. So I didn’t realize it. And I tell people if I would have known I probably would have fainted. And it’s better that I didn’t realize. But it was really interesting to know things, and I came right in the club and played the music, and I mean everything was fine.
